blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant tsiko. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

This guide shows how Filipino growers usually plant chico from a marcot or a grafted seedling and care for it until the first fruits. It is for backyards and small orchards, mostly with the common Pineras and the big fruited Ponderosa.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for fruit and plantation trees](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation). Then choose your seed or planting material with the [tsiko varieties sold here](/crop-varieties/chico). If the leaves turn pale later on, the [tsiko nutrient deficiency guide](/nutrient-deficiencies/chico-nutrient-deficiency) helps you find what is missing. For more on the crop, read [pagtatanim ng puno](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-puno).
When to plant tsiko

Marcots and grafted seedlings are planted as the rains begin, around May to July. Chico stands drier places better than most fruit trees, and in the Philippines it flowers most around April to June, with the main harvest about December to February.
What you plant

In the old way growers make their own marcots: in the rainy season they girdle a fairly upright branch about 1 cm thick on a good bearing tree, wrap it in moist coir or soil and plastic, and cut it once roots fill the wrap, which can take 4 to 12 months. Many nurseries now sell cleft grafted seedlings on seedling rootstock. Trees from seed are slow to bear and many give poor crops.
Paano magtanim ng chico, step by step

Marcotted chico usually starts bearing at about 3 to 4 years and grafted trees at about 4 to 6 years. Fruits take about 6 to 8 months from flowering to maturity. The crop is ready about 4 years after planting.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 14 days before planting: Mark and dig the holes
items.text: Mark the planting spots about 6 to 10 m apart, wider for big trees. Dig holes wider than the bag and mix the topsoil with compost or manure for filling back.

blocks.text: The nursery (Punlaan)

items.title: 8 months before planting: Make the marcot
items.text: In the rainy season, pick a healthy, fairly upright branch about 1 cm thick on a heavy bearing tree. Peel a ring of bark, wrap the cut with moist coir or soil in plastic and tie both ends.

items.title: 2 months before planting: Cut and pot the rooted marcot
items.text: When roots show all through the wrap, cut the branch below it, remove the plastic and plant it in a bag of loose soil. Keep it in light shade and water it until new leaves come.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Planting day: Plant at the start of the rains
items.text: Remove the bag without breaking the soil ball and set the plant at the same depth. Fill in, press the soil, water well and tie the young tree to a stake against wind.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 1: Water in dry spells
items.text: Water the new tree whenever a dry spell comes until it is well rooted, and mulch around the base. Shade it lightly for the first weeks if the sun is harsh.

items.title: Day 30: Weed and give the first feeding
items.text: Keep a clean circle around the tree and give it a little complete fertilizer or manure, spread in a ring and covered. Feed at the start and again before the end of the rains each year, more as it grows.

items.title: Month 4: Check for pests
items.text: Look at new shoots and fruits for mealybugs, scale insects and fruit borers, and cut off and burn badly hit twigs. Keep fallen leaves and fruit cleaned up.

items.title: Month 12: Light shaping only
items.text: Chico needs little pruning since flowers come near the shoot tips. On upright trees cut back the main leader early so side branches form, and later remove low branches that touch the ground.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Year 4: First fruits
items.text: Pick when the skin turns from green to yellowish brown, the brown powder rubs off easily with the thumb and little sap flows when the fruit is pulled off. Soak the fruits in water so the sap bleeds out, scrub off the powder and let them ripen in 3 to 7 days.

blocks.text: Spacing, water and fertilizer for tsiko
Spacing

About 6 to 10 m between trees, one plant a hole. Some growers use about 9 m between rows and 6 to 7 m in the row. Planting two varieties near each other helps fruit set, since some kinds need pollen from another tree.
Water

Mostly rain fed. New trees are watered in dry spells until they take hold. Bearing trees in dry places do better with water during flowering and fruit growth, since flowers and young fruits drop when the soil is too dry.
Fertilizer

Compost or manure in the hole. Young trees get a little complete fertilizer or manure at the start and again before the end of the rains, more each year. Grown trees need a lot of nitrogen with some phosphorus and potash, spread in a ring under the edge of the canopy at the same two times. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-fruit-trees).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows

Staking and mulching young trees, weeding a circle around them, very light pruning, removing sagging low branches, and checking for mealybugs, scale and fruit borers. Bees help set fruit, so growers avoid harming them.
When and how to harvest

Fruits take about 6 to 8 months from flowering to maturity, and the main crop in the Philippines comes about December to February. Mature fruits are yellowish brown, the brown bloom rubs off easily, and little sap flows when the fruit is pulled off. Growers test a few first. After picking, the fruits are soaked so the sap bleeds out, scrubbed, dried stalk end down and left to ripen in 3 to 7 days.
Common mistakes when planting tsiko

items: Planting seedlings from seed, which take many years and often bear poorly.
Picking fruits that are still green under the bloom, so they never ripen sweet.
Skipping the soak after picking, so sap hardens inside the fruit.
Pruning hard, which cuts off the shoot tips where flowers form.
Planting a lone Ponderosa tree with no other variety nearby for pollen.
Letting young trees dry out in their first dry season.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of tsiko
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Use marcots or grafted seedlings from a proven, heavy bearing tree or an accredited nursery.
Test the soil and feed by the result, twice a year at the start and end of the rains.
Water during flowering and fruit growth in dry places to stop flower and fruit drop.
Plant two or more varieties near each other for better fruit set.
Scout for mealybugs, scale and fruit borers and clean up fallen fruit.
Sort and bleed the fruits right after picking for a better price.
